title: The digital economy is shifting from access expansion toward capability, agency, resilience, and strategic fragmentation
source_unit: Digital Cooperation Organization, Digital Economy Trends 2026, third edition
geography: Global digital economy, regional readiness comparisons, and expert survey perspectives across public, private, and societal stakeholders

observations.period: 2026 report; 18 forces shaping the next digital-economy era

denominator.unit: digital-economy forces identified by the DCO report

force_set.value: vertical AI, generalist robots, sustainable digital infrastructure, ambient intelligence, frontier-tech convergence, competing technology blocs, digital trade, immersive experiences, AI divide, digital sovereignty, quantum, workforce transformation, brain-machine interfaces, digital well-being, cybersecurity, agentic AI, API-enabled collaboration, and hyper-personalization

strategic_shift.value: from expanding access toward strengthening the capacity, agency, and resilience of individuals and nations

observations.method: DCO horizon-scanning and expert-informed synthesis of digital-economy trends, impacts, readiness, and policy implications.
observations.uncertainty: A trend framework identifies plausible forces and priorities but does not establish their probability, causal effects, or equal relevance across countries and sectors.
observations.subgroup: Individuals, societies, governments, private firms, technology companies, workers, and sectors with different levels of digital capability and infrastructure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some listed forces may remain niche, converge differently, or generate benefits through existing institutions without becoming dominant social or economic trends.

observations.period: 2026; expected global digital-economy impact over the next 3-5 years

denominator.unit: DCO expert outlook on the global digital economy

access_outlook.value: experts expect digital goods and services to become more accessible and affordable

concentration_risk.value: AI advances may concentrate among a few large companies and widen the gap between returns to capital and labor

resilience_condition.value: greater interconnection makes resilience and trust necessary to realize positive economic, social, and environmental effects

observations.method: DCO expert outlook and synthesis of affordability, concentration, labor, and resilience implications.
observations.uncertainty: The outlook is expectation-based and does not quantify future prices, concentration, labor displacement, or who captures gains.
observations.subgroup: Consumers, workers, firms, technology providers, governments, and communities facing different costs and benefits from digital scale.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower digital prices can broaden access, while competition policy, public investment, open standards, and labor institutions can alter concentration and distributional outcomes.

observations.period: 2026; regional trend impact and readiness assessment

denominator.unit: regional comparisons presented by the DCO report

highest_impact_trend.value: end-to-end cybersecurity is broadly identified as having the greatest potential socio-economic impact

readiness_pattern.value: three of five regions record their highest readiness score in cybersecurity

positive_impact_horizon.value: intelligent systems embedded in daily life and expanded digital trade are among the trends expected to create positive impact in the next 12-18 months

observations.method: DCO regional comparison of expert-rated socio-economic impact and stakeholder readiness.
observations.uncertainty: Regional readiness scores are perception-based and may not measure operational capability, actual cyber incidents, or realized benefits; five-region comparisons are not country-level evaluations.
observations.subgroup: Regions, public agencies, firms, individuals, digital infrastructure operators, and communities exposed to different security and capability conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: High perceived readiness may reflect awareness rather than capacity, while low perceived readiness can coexist with effective local practice or rapidly improving institutions.

observations.period: 2026; expected private-sector employment and preparedness over the next 12-18 months

denominator.unit: DCO survey respondent outlook on employment and stakeholder preparedness

headcount_expectation.unit: average percent expected increase in company headcounts

employment_balance.value: more experts foresee digital trends expanding than reducing employment, while 60 percent expect no more than a slight effect either way

prepared_private.unit: percent saying private-sector stakeholders are prepared

prepared_public_and_society.value: 70 percent for the public sector and 43 percent for societies and individuals

observations.method: DCO expert survey synthesis of employment expectations and perceived preparedness across private, public, and societal stakeholders.
observations.uncertainty: Expectations and preparedness perceptions are not realized employment outcomes, organizational audits, or population-representative measures; the headcount estimate does not identify sector, geography, or job-quality effects.
observations.subgroup: Private firms, public institutions, societies and individuals, workers, managers, and sectors undergoing different technology transitions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Perceived private-sector preparedness may coexist with worker insecurity or public capacity; modest aggregate headcount change can conceal displacement, reclassification, or unequal job quality.

related_sources.claim: DCO describes the Digital Economy Trends series as evidence-based analysis of global digital-economy trends, technologies, and policy considerations.
ITU ICT Development Index 2026 provides complementary connectivity, affordability, and quality measures across 159 economies.

boundary: This record adds a global digital-economy foresight and readiness route linking AI, automation, energy, data, cybersecurity, trade, sovereignty, work, digital well-being, and social agency. It is an expert-informed publication and survey synthesis, not a technology forecast, firm census, individual employment panel, causal employment estimate, or proof that preparedness produces equitable outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: DCO Digital Economy Trends 2026 landing page and DCO report overview were reviewed for the 18-force framework, impact and readiness comparisons, employment expectations, and preparedness claims.
